source.title: Overcoming Sparsity Artifacts in Crosscoders to Interpret Chat-Tuning
source.authors: Julian Minder; Clément Dumas; C. Juang; Bilal Chughtai; Neel Nanda

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. The text contains some extraction/formatting artifacts, but the relevant results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares crosscoder sparsity objectives and reports that L1 training can put latent information in reconstruction error, while BatchTopK largely mitigates the identified attribution artifacts. It also tests the behavioral information in reconstruction-error-based approximations.
record.gate_note: The paper's main crosscoder experiments compare latent attribution and behavioral KL effects; they are not direct tests of SAE error linear predictability, error-norm scaling across SAE sizes, or matched random errors. Training statistics and hyperparameters are not separate outcome rows. Results cited from prior work are excluded.
record.test_reason: In a crosscoder setting (an SAE variant on stacked base and chat activations), the study measures how much chat-model behaviour (output KL) is lost without the chat reconstruction error, and compares this across L1 and BatchTopK objectives. Its error-ratio analysis also shows the L1 penalty pushing latent information into the error. This bears on V5 and V6 in a new setting; it is not the original method.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, with one omission. The authors conclude that the L1 crosscoder loss creates spurious chat-only latents through Complete Shrinkage and Latent Decoupling, and that BatchTopK largely removes these artifacts. They also state that both crosscoders capture the behavioural difference about equally. Even for BatchTopK, the reconstruction error still holds much chat-behaviour information: as much as the dictionary over full responses, but less on early tokens.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares L1 and BatchTopK crosscoders for model diffing and uses activation replacements with output KL divergence. It does not reproduce the original SAE error-prediction or per-token scaling measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported error-term contribution changes between full responses and the first nine analyzed response tokens. Error-related latent attribution also differs between L1 and BatchTopK crosscoder objectives.
record.problems: The evidence concerns crosscoders rather than standalone SAEs and uses KL divergence rather than model loss against matched-size random errors. Main causal experiments use 512 chat interactions, and the paper reports 95% confidence intervals without giving their exact values in the text. The authors also note that analysis focused on small models' middle layers.
record.rows_left_out: None of the directly relevant error-term and error-ratio outcomes were left out. Other latent-ranking, interpretability, and steering outcomes were excluded because they do not measure reconstruction-error behavior for the claim versions.

untested.parts: Linear predictability of the error from input activations is not measured.
Per-token error-norm scaling across dictionary sizes and failure on shared contexts are not measured.
There is no comparison against random errors of matched norm.
There is no split of the error into linear and nonlinear components, and no test of further dictionary learning.
Circuit and steering analyses with versus without the error term are not run. Effects are measured only as output KL at one middle layer of small models.
Not tested: end-to-end training, dead-latent effects, and whether dark matter tracks model structure beyond the two sparsity objectives compared.

missing.what: Fraction of variance explained by L1 versus BatchTopK crosscoders: Gemma validation 84.6% vs 87.6% total FVE; Llama 3.2 1B and 3.1 8B 76.5-76.6% vs 81.5%. This shows error magnitude shrinks only modestly with the better objective.
Cross-architecture comparison as a V6 test: the All replacement KL reduction is almost identical for L1 and BatchTopK, so the behaviourally relevant error does not shrink with the better objective.
Replication of the All/None KL baselines on LMSYS-CHAT for the L1 crosscoder (qualitatively same trends).
Error-ratio (complete shrinkage) replications for L1 versus BatchTopK on Llama 3.2 1B, Llama 3.1 8B, Meditron and Nemotron pairs, and on Kissane et al.'s independently trained L1 crosscoder.
missing.locator: Appendix I, Table 1, Figures 14-18; Appendix J

record.verdict_notes: The subject is crosscoders, not standalone SAEs, so V5 and V6 evidence is a related setting (T3). The original dark-matter paper (Engels et al.) is cited only to align with the error-causality result. The V6 picture is mixed. The objective-induced shrinkage is a training artifact that BatchTopK fixes, but the behaviourally relevant error persists across objectives, which runs against V6's broader claim. Figure 4's numeric labels are garbled in the extracted text, so exact KL values were not assigned to bars.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure how much of an SAE error vector is linearly predictable from its input activation.
It does not compare per-token error norms across SAE sizes, test whether larger SAEs fail on the same tokens, or measure whether error vanishes with scale.
It does not compare model loss after SAE reconstruction replacement with matched-size random errors.

It distinguishes shrinkage and latent-decoupling effects in crosscoders, but does not test the claimed linear and nonlinear components of SAE dark matter or their response to further dictionary learning.
The study measures KL divergence for crosscoder-derived approximations, not the effect of omitting error in specific circuit or steering analyses, nor behavior beyond the tested model outputs.
The study examines L1 and BatchTopK crosscoder error-related latent attribution, not SAE end-to-end training, random-error comparisons, or whether total error magnitude shrinks across architectures.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B base + Gemma-2-2b-it chat (L1 crosscoder)
rows.operation_detail: Compared KL divergence for full replacement of crosscoder latents with the None baseline (base activation).

conditions.value: 512 chat interactions from Ding et al.'s dataset; chat-model-generated responses

rows.measure: KL divergence reduction relative to None
rows.baseline: None (base activation); exact KL value not stated here
rows.value: All replacement reduced KL divergence by 59% compared with None; the two crosscoder architectures were reported as almost identical.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals shown in Figure 4; exact intervals not stated
rows.note: The reduction shows that learned dictionary representations recover some behavioral difference, but not all of it.
rows.check: Recoding from partial. All replacement (chat reconstruction + base error, i.e. dropping the chat error) recovers only 59% of the KL gap on full responses. About 41% of the behavioural difference is lost without the error term, which is the V5 effect. Exact KL values are in Figure 4 but garbled in the text.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B base + Gemma-2-2b-it chat (L1 crosscoder)
rows.operation_detail: Measured error ratios for chat-only latents to assess complete shrinkage under L1 crosscoder training.
rows.baseline: Shared latents, for which high error ratios were expected; exact values not stated
rows.value: Chat-only latents had high error ratios, up to approximately 0.5.
rows.note: The authors interpret high error ratios as evidence that L1 shrinkage left latent information in the reconstruction error.
rows.check: Bears on V6 only for the shrinkage component. The L1 penalty leaves chat-only latents' base information in the error (error ratio up to about 0.5). This is a per-latent attribution measure, not the size of the error.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1, opening paragraph and discussion of Figure 2a.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B base + Gemma-2-2b-it chat (BatchTopK crosscoder)
rows.operation_detail: Measured error ratios for chat-only latents to assess complete shrinkage under BatchTopK crosscoder training.
rows.baseline: Shared latents, for which high error ratios were expected; exact values not stated
rows.value: Error ratios were nearly zero, indicating minimal complete shrinkage.
rows.note: This is a crosscoder architecture comparison, not a measurement of total SAE reconstruction-error magnitude.
rows.check: Recoding from absent. Measured against V6, the near-zero error ratios show the objective-induced shrinkage disappearing under BatchTopK, which is what V6 predicts for this component. The row is a comparator to R9.

relationships.condition: Gemma 2 2B base/chat, layer 13, both L1 and BatchTopK crosscoders, full responses and tokens 2-10
relationships.reason: Dropping the chat error leaves 41% (full responses) and 22% (tokens 2-10) of the KL gap unrecovered (R1-R4). On full responses the error alone recovers slightly more than the dictionary (R5, R6).
relationships.display_finding: Dropping the chat error left 41% of the KL gap unrecovered across full responses and 22% across tokens 2–10; across full responses, the error alone recovered slightly more than the dictionary.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Gemma 2 2B base/chat, layer 13, both L1 and BatchTopK crosscoders, full responses and tokens 2-10
source_check.reason: R1–R4 leave substantial output KL unrecovered by All replacement; R5–R6 independently show substantial information recoverable through chat-error replacement.

relationships.reason: Early in the response, the error-only replacement does more than twice worse than the dictionary replacement. The error's behavioural share depends on token position (R7, R8).
relationships.display_finding: Error-only replacement performed more than twice as poorly as dictionary replacement, showing that the error's behavioral contribution varied with token position.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: R7–R8 show that error replacement is less effective than dictionary replacement early in responses. V5 does not require error to outperform the dictionary; approximately 22% of baseline KL remains unrecovered by All, supporting meaningful error dependence.

relationships.condition: Chat-only latents, L1 versus BatchTopK crosscoder
relationships.reason: The L1 sparsity penalty pushes latent information into the base error (error ratio up to about 0.5), and BatchTopK nearly eliminates this. Part of the error content is a training artifact (R9, R10).
relationships.display_finding: L1 pushed chat-only latent information into base reconstruction error, with error ratios reaching about 0.5; BatchTopK nearly eliminated this leakage.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Chat-only latents, L1 versus BatchTopK crosscoder
source_check.reason: R9–R10 support the training-artifact component: L1 leaves latent information in base error, whereas BatchTopK nearly eliminates this specific shrinkage effect. They do not establish that most total error is an artifact.

relationships.condition: Behaviourally relevant error, L1 versus BatchTopK on Gemma 2 2B
relationships.reason: Based on the text: both objectives leave almost the same behaviour in the error (59% and 78% recovery each, R1-R4). The authors say the BatchTopK error terms 'still contain a lot of information' about chat behaviour.
relationships.display_finding: L1 and BatchTopK errors yielded nearly identical behavioral recovery, at 59% and 78% in the respective evaluations, retaining substantial chat information.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: Behaviourally relevant error, L1 versus BatchTopK on Gemma 2 2B
source_check.reason: Removing the shrinkage artifact does not materially improve All-replacement KL recovery: both objectives report approximately 59% and 78%. Figure 4 and Section 5 show substantial functional information remaining in BatchTopK error.

tranche.reason: The study tests functional reconstruction error and training-induced error content in the new setting of base/chat crosscoders.

source_check.notes: Figure 2 contains an instruction addressed to reviewers; it was ignored. The 41% and 22% figures are arithmetic complements of reported KL reductions, not additive shares of all model behaviour; latent error ratios measure a separate construct.

statements.correction: Error replacement outperforms All over full responses and underperforms All on tokens 2–10; All still leaves approximately 22% of baseline KL unrecovered on early tokens. V5 remains supported in that condition.
statements.problem: The replacement ranking changes as stated, but this does not establish a condition where V5's meaningful error dependence fails.

statements.correction: All replacement = chat reconstruction + base error; reported KL reductions relative to None: approximately 59% over full responses and 78% over tokens 2–10 for both objectives. Error replacement = base reconstruction + chat error; separate intervention. BatchTopK errors retain substantial chat-behaviour information.
statements.problem: The condition attributes the 59% and 78% recovery values to error-term replacements; those values describe All replacement.
